m-supraspinatus.summary: The upper member of the rotator cuff, filling the fossa above the spine of the scapula. It initiates abduction.
facts: Supraspinous fossa of the scapula
Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus and the joint capsule
Suprascapular nerve (C5–C6)
Suprascapular artery
Initiates abduction of the arm (first 15°); holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity
clinical: It is the most commonly torn and impinged rotator cuff muscle; its tendon is trapped under the acromion.
The 'empty can' test assesses supraspinatus; a painful arc between 60° and 120° of abduction is typical.
tus: Supraspinatus test: the 'empty can' (Jobe) test; the drop-arm test indicates a complete tear.
Calcific tendinitis is most common in the supraspinatus tendon.

m-infraspinatus.summary: A thick triangular muscle filling the fossa below the spine of the scapula; a member of the rotator cuff.
facts: Infraspinous fossa of the scapula
Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
Suprascapular nerve (C5–C6)
Suprascapular artery, circumflex scapular artery
Rotates the arm outwards (external rotation); stabilises the head of the humerus in the glenoid
clinical: Compression of the suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch can cause wasting of infraspinatus alone (in volleyball players).
tus: Infraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve; compression at the spinoglenoid notch affects infraspinatus alone.

m-teres-minor.summary: A small cylindrical muscle running from the lateral border of the scapula to the humerus; a member of the rotator cuff.
facts: Upper 2/3 of the lateral border of the scapula
Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
Axillary nerve (C5–C6)
Circumflex scapular artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery
Rotates the arm outwards and adducts it slightly; stabilises the head of the humerus
sections: Triangular and quadrangular spaces are formed between teres minor, teres major, the long head of triceps and the humerus; the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery pass through the quadrangular space.
tus: Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve; it forms the upper boundary of the quadrangular space.

m-subscapularis.summary: A large triangular muscle covering the anterior (costal) surface of the scapula; the strongest member of the rotator cuff.
facts: Subscapular fossa
Lesser tubercle of the humerus
Upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5–C7)
Subscapular artery, suprascapular artery
Rotates the arm inwards (internal rotation) and adducts it; prevents forward displacement of the head of the humerus
clinical: The lift-off (Gerber) test and belly-press test assess the integrity of subscapularis.
tus: Subscapularis is the largest and strongest muscle of the rotator cuff; it plays a major role in anterior stability.

m-teres-major.summary: A thick muscle running from the inferior angle of the scapula to the humerus; it works together with latissimus dorsi (latissimus's little helper).
facts: Posterior surface of the inferior angle of the scapula
Crest of the lesser tubercle of the humerus (medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus)
Lower subscapular nerve (C5–C7)
Circumflex scapular artery, thoracodorsal artery
Adducts, internally rotates and extends the arm
tus: The lower border of teres major is where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery.

m-biceps-brachii.summary: The prominent two-headed muscle on the front of the arm. It crosses both the shoulder and the elbow joints and is the most powerful supinator of the forearm.
facts: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula; short head: coracoid process
Radial tuberosity and, via the bicipital aponeurosis, the deep fascia of the forearm
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6)
Muscular branches of the brachial artery
Flexes the forearm and supinates it (corkscrew movement); assists flexion of the arm
clinical: When the long head tendon ruptures, the muscle belly bunches up distally (Popeye sign).
The biceps reflex tests segments C5–C6.
The brachial artery and median nerve run beneath the bicipital aponeurosis; the median cubital vein used for blood sampling lies on top of it.
tus: The biceps reflex assesses C5–C6, mainly C5.
The bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus) covers and protects the brachial artery and median nerve.

m-brachialis.summary: A thick muscle beneath biceps, in front of the lower half of the humerus. It is the main flexor of the elbow.
facts: Lower half of the anterior surface of the humerus
Coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6); its lateral part also receives fibres from the radial nerve
Brachial artery, radial collateral artery
Flexes the forearm in every position (the 'workhorse' of elbow flexion)
clinical: After elbow fractures, ectopic ossification may develop within the muscle (myositis ossificans).
tus: Post-traumatic ossification in brachialis (myositis ossificans) may follow elbow fractures.

m-coracobrachialis.summary: A slender muscle of the anterior compartment of the arm running from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it.
facts: Coracoid process of the scapula
Middle of the medial surface of the shaft of the humerus
Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7)
Brachial artery
Flexes and adducts the arm; stabilises the head of the humerus
tus: Coracobrachialis flexes and adducts the arm; the musculocutaneous nerve piercing it is an important landmark.

m-triceps-brachii.summary: A three-headed muscle occupying the entire posterior compartment of the arm. It is the main extensor of the elbow.
facts: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula; lateral head: above the radial groove; medial head: below the radial groove
Olecranon of the ulna
Radial nerve (C6–C8)
Profunda brachii artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery
Extends the forearm; the long head assists extension and adduction of the arm
clinical: The triceps reflex tests segment C7.
If the radial nerve is injured at mid-humerus, part of the medial head may be spared; in high lesions in the axilla triceps is completely paralysed.
tus: The long head of triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle and also crosses the shoulder.
The triceps reflex assesses segment C7.

m-anconeus.summary: A small triangular muscle on the posterolateral aspect of the elbow; it works like a continuation of triceps.
facts: Posterior surface of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Lateral surface of the olecranon and upper part of the posterior surface of the ulna
Radial nerve (C7–C8)
Recurrent interosseous artery
Assists elbow extension; tenses the joint capsule and stabilises the ulna during pronation
tus: Anconeus assists elbow extension and is supplied by the radial nerve; it tenses the lateral capsule of the elbow.

m-pronator-teres.summary: A muscle of the upper anterior forearm running obliquely from the elbow to the middle of the radius. The median nerve passes between its two heads.
facts: Humeral head: medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon); ulnar head: coronoid process of the ulna
Middle of the lateral surface of the radius (pronator tuberosity)
Median nerve (C6–C7)
Ulnar and radial arteries
Pronates the forearm; assists elbow flexion
clinical: Compression of the median nerve between the two heads (pronator teres syndrome) mimics carpal tunnel syndrome but also causes numbness of the palm.
tus: The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres, the ulnar artery beneath the deep (ulnar) head.
In pronator syndrome palmar sensation is also affected (unlike carpal tunnel).

m-flexor-carpi-radialis.summary: One of the superficial muscles of the anterior forearm; at the wrist its tendon is felt just medial to the radial pulse.
facts: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
Bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals
Median nerve (C6–C7)
Radial artery
Flexes the wrist and deviates it radially (abduction)
sections: The radial pulse is taken just lateral to its tendon at the wrist.
tus: The FCR tendon is a landmark at the wrist just medial to the radial artery.

m-palmaris-longus.summary: A forearm muscle with a thin, long tendon that is absent in about 14% of people.
facts: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
Flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis
Median nerve (C7–C8)
Ulnar artery
Assists wrist flexion; tenses the palmar aponeurosis
clinical: Its tendon is often used as a tendon graft.
At the wrist the median nerve runs just beneath and lateral to this tendon.
tus: The presence of palmaris longus is tested by touching the tips of the thumb and little finger together and flexing the wrist.

m-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.summary: A superficial flexor on the anteromedial border of the forearm; one of the two anterior forearm muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve.
facts: Humeral head: medial epicondyle of the humerus; ulnar head: olecranon and posterior border of the ulna
Pisiform, hook of the hamate and base of the 5th metacarpal
Ulnar nerve (C7–T1)
Ulnar artery
Flexes the wrist and deviates it to the ulnar side (adduction)
clinical: The ulnar nerve can be compressed in the cubital tunnel between its two heads (cubital tunnel syndrome).
tus: The ulnar nerve can be compressed in the cubital tunnel between the two heads of FCU.
